_meta: Two light layers given as normalized RGB (channels in 0..1), used to show that combining light sources -- a glow, a lens flare, two lamps, an additive particle effect -- with plain addition clips at pure white and destroys information wherever the lights are already bright, while the screen operator brightens like light but stays inside the range and never clips. Additive blend is a+b: it is physically the way light energy sums, but a display channel maxes out at 1.0, so any sum above 1.0 is clamped to 1.0, and every overlap that would have summed to 1.3 or 1.7 becomes the same flat white -- the bright regions blow out and lose all their variation and hue. The screen operator is 1 - (1-a)(1-b): it also brightens (the result is at least as bright as either input), it is commutative so the order of the layers does not matter (unlike the alpha 'over' operator, which occludes and is order-dependent), and it asymptotes toward 1 without ever exceeding it, so bright-on-bright stays distinct instead of collapsing to white. On this fixture a warm layer and a cool layer overlap: added, the red and blue channels exceed 1.0 and clamp, so the overlap is a blown-out near-white; screened, the same overlap is a brighter but still-colored value with every channel below 1.0. A separate collision demo shows two different additive sums that both clamp to 1.0 -- indistinguishable -- while screen keeps them distinct. The two layers and two collision pairs are the fixture; every additive sum, clamp, screen value, and the range, accumulation, commutativity, and collision checks are computed. Stdlib only.
